extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, law students, and judges interested in specification requirements
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for preparing and evaluating a patent specification: what must be disclosed, how clearly, and what omissions or ambiguities will invalidate a patent. Draws on English case law examples and statutory rules (including disclaimers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Object of the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The object of the specification is, that after the term has expired the public shall have the benefit of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification's purpose is to teach the public how to practice the invention once the patent expires; disclosure must therefore be sufficient for that public benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full disclosure / no material falsehoods
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification is intended to teach the public; it must fully disclose the secret, and contain nothing materially false or defective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not omit material means or supply false statements. Examples: omission of a material process step (e.g., use of tallow) can render the specification bad. The specification must not mislead the public about how to practice the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement / sufficiency for persons skilled in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification ought to be so clearly worded as to enable any person of sufficient understanding on the particular subject to attain the result without doubt or difficulty; it must be sufficient for persons skilled in the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test: a competent workman, possessing ordinary (not extraordinary) skill, should be able to make/use the invention by following the specification without further invention or additions. The general test: directions must enable construction/operation without new inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode / most advantageous mode known
rubrics_metrics.description: It is required, as the price of the monopoly, that the patentee should enrol to the very best of his knowledge and judgment, the fullest and most sufficient description of the particulars on which the effect depended; the most advantageous mode known to the inventor, and any circumstance conducive to the advantageous operation, must be stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose the best mode known at the time of enrolment; improvements discovered during the interval for enrolling should be described. Failure to disclose the best mode may vitiate the patent or lead to loss of remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: State materials/compositions/proportions when essential
rubrics_metrics.description: The compositions and proportions, where materials and quantity are of the essence of the invention, must be given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention depends on specific materials or proportions (e.g., medicines, paints), list them with necessary detail. Omitting essential compositional data is fatal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe material alterations to existing apparatus
rubrics_metrics.description: Any material alteration to be made in existing apparatus or machines must be stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the invention modifies existing apparatus (materials, form, speed, relative dimensions), those material changes must be described; concealing such alterations can invalidate the patent (Arkwright examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe new parts and their mode of operation
rubrics_metrics.description: Every part of the invention which is new must be accurately described, as to the manner in which it is to operate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe how new parts work and interact. Example: if rollers must have different textures/velocities for intended effect, the spec must state it (Felton v. Greaves). Failing to describe operational details can render the specification insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must state at least one method which will succeed
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification must state at least one method which will succeed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not enough to suggest possibilities; provide at least one concrete, workable method. A specification that only causes the public to engage in trial-and-error is bad.

rubrics_metrics.name: No requirement that described apparatus be the best possible
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary that the apparatus described should produce the greatest amount of benefit; it is sufficient if persons acquainted with the art would construct an apparatus productive of some benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification need not claim the optimal embodiment; a working, beneficial embodiment that a skilled person can build suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not require information from other sources / avoid undue experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Information must not be requisite from other sources. If experiments are necessary for the production of any beneficial effects, the patent is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All necessary details to practice the invention should be in the specification (except routine skill). If practicing the invention would require external undisclosed knowledge or extensive experimentation, the specification is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of matters within ordinary knowledge is acceptable; omission of what patentee knows necessary is fatal
rubrics_metrics.description: The omission to give directions as to matters within the knowledge of a workman, who would, under ordinary circumstances be employed to carry out the invention, is no ground of invalidity. But the omission to mention anything which the patentee knows to be necessary for the beneficial enjoyment of his invention is a fatal defect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not burden the specification with routine trade knowledge, but do disclose anything you know is essential to make the invention work. Courts distinguish between ordinary skill and inventor-known necessities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish what is new and what is old
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must inform the public what is new and what old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearly identify novel features versus previously known elements. Failure to do so may lead to the patent being construed as claiming the whole apparatus or parts that are old.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous or generic terms that mislead
rubrics_metrics.description: If the terms in which the description of the subject is expressed be ambiguous...the grant would be invalid. Use of generic terms where only one species works (e.g., 'fossil salt' vs 'sal gem') can make the specification bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise in naming materials and limits. Examples: claiming 'any other substance' can be fatal if the embodiment only works with a narrower set; technical terms with nonstandard meanings should be explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not insert parts or descriptions solely to puzzle or mislead
rubrics_metrics.description: The representation and description of parts of no use, or without distinguishing to what purposes they are to be applied, or for the purpose of puzzling, will render the patent void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid including irrelevant or deceptive material in drawings or descriptions. Every described part should have a clear purpose or be identified as known/old.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plainest and easiest mode of production must be stated; avoid concealment by obscure terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The plainest and most easy way of production must be stated, and if obscure terms be employed for the sake of concealment, so as to induce the belief that elaborate processes are necessary, when the simplest will succeed, the specification is bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose the straightforward way to make the invention; do not cloak basic steps in technical obscurity to hide the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical terms are acceptable if addressed to skilled persons; explain if using nonstandard meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: It is no objection prima facie to a specification, that it contains terms of art requiring explanation. A specification containing scientific terms which are not understood except by persons acquainted with the nature of the business, is not bad, provided a scientific person does understand them; but if a common term is used in a nontechnical way and would mislead a common person, it should be explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use trade/scientific language appropriate for skilled readers, but clarify when a term is used in a specialized or unusual sense (examples: 'malt' meaning barley fully prepared).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistakes and verbal inaccuracies not necessarily fatal if cannot mislead
rubrics_metrics.description: A mistake in a specification does not of necessity vitiate letters-patent... Semble, that a mistake in respect of a matter foreign to the invention, and which cannot mislead, will not vitiate the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context may cure inadvertent misstatements; courts may allow correction where the mistake is non-material and cannot mislead skilled persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of description is a jury question (fact-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sufficiency of the specification in matters of description is a question for the jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether a specification is sufficiently descriptive depends on evidence (e.g., whether persons were misled); factual findings (jury) are conclusive on distinctness/clarity issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification should warn the public what is prohibited and teach the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification is to warn the public of what is prohibited, and to teach them the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims/description should clearly demarcate the patentee's exclusion (what the public must avoid) and provide teaching sufficient for use by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common defects in specifications (summary list)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification is bad, when: 1. The terms are ambiguous. 2. Necessary descriptions are omitted. 3. Parts claimed are not original. 4. Things are put in to mislead. 5. The drawings are incorrect. 6. One of different ways, or different ingredients named, fails. 7. One of several effects specified is not produced. 8. The things described are not the best known to the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist when reviewing a specification. Each item is illustrated by cases in the text (e.g., ambiguous 'fossil salt', omitted necessary steps, misleading extra parts, failing species in a claimed class).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory disclaimer formalities and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Any such patentee...may make disclaimers of such parts of the thing patented...which disclaimer shall be in writing, attested by one or more witnesses, and recorded in the patent office, on payment... of the sum of ten dollars... such disclaimer shall thereafter be taken and considered as part of the original specification... But no such disclaimer shall affect any action pending at the time of its being filed, except so far as may relate to the question of unreasonable neglect or delay in filing the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclaimers must follow statutory formalities (writing, witnesses, recording, fee) and become part of the specification; their effect differs depending on whether suits are pending when filed (7th section) or suits are brought after filing (9th section). Failure to enter required disclaimer prior to suit may affect entitlement to costs and equitable relief; unreasonable delay/neglect can bar benefits.
